title: The Torah in Greek
hookLine: the Torah is translated into Greek; legend says by seventy-two elders
carry: something always stays behind in the original

cards: A king sends for seventy-two elders. That's how the Talmud tells it, in tractate Megillah. King Ptolemy gathers them, and before they can talk to each other, he puts each one in a separate house.
He doesn't tell them why. Then he goes to each man alone: write for me the Torah of Moses your teacher. In Greek.
Seventy-two rooms, seventy-two pens, no way to compare notes. Anyone who has translated knows the problem: a sentence can have more than one right answer. So what comes out of those rooms?

teach.b: The same thing, every time. The Talmud says God put wisdom in each one's heart, and all of them agreed. Each made the same small changes, where a word-for-word Greek version might be misread by a king.
The very first line is one.

Hebrew opens with in the beginning, then created, then God. Read too literally, a Greek reader might think in the beginning was the one doing the creating. So all seventy-two wrote God created in the beginning.

In the legend, careful translation is a kind of guarding. And the rabbis had more than one feeling about it. In the Mishnah, Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says that besides Hebrew, the holy books may be written in Greek.
The Talmud finds a reason in Noah's blessing, in the King James words: "God shall enlarge Japheth, and he shall dwell in the tents of Shem."
The rabbis read it as the beauty of Japheth, the Greek language, dwelling in the tents of Shem, Israel's house of study.

teach.h: A GIFT, AND A HARD DAY.
teach.b: But the minor tractate Soferim remembers a Greek translation made for King Ptolemy as a hard day, as hard for Israel as the day the golden calf was made, because the Torah could not be fully translated.
A gift that lets the Torah travel. A loss, because something always stays behind in the original. Anyone reading a verse in English today stands inside that old argument.

how: Jews today read the Torah in Hebrew in the synagogue and study it in many languages, often with a translation printed beside the Hebrew; the Talmud's story of the seventy-two elders is taught in tractate Megillah.

practice: Take one verse, Noah's blessing from today if nothing else is at hand, and read it slowly. Which word might be carrying something it can't quite hold?
If you know a little Hebrew, look at the Hebrew too; if you pray, give thanks for whoever carried this text into your language.

wordCard.voice: Megillah, the Talmud tractate that tells how seventy-two elders in separate rooms all wrote the same Greek translation of the Torah. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: the Greek language, the one tongue the Mishnah's Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel allows besides Hebrew for holy books.

carryVoice: Your line: something always stays behind in the original. That ends a week that began with three parts, one library, then a doubt didn't throw a book out, plain meaning first, where the verse breathes is where its thought divides, the pages ran out, the handing-on didn't, and two cultures meet. Day eight hundred eighty-nine.
